overview: Noongar communities in southwestern Australia connect Country, family, language and cultural responsibilities. Their traditions continue through elders, families and community organisations.

items.text: Noongar Protocols describes distinct language groups with their own laws, customs and relationships to Country. Noongar identity should not be represented as one historical kingdom.
Caring for Country accompanies hunting, fishing and gathering. Environmental responsibilities form part of social and spiritual life.
Stories, art, song and dance transmit knowledge and responsibilities between generations. Ceremonies also sustain relationships within communities.
Recognised elders or community representatives conduct Welcome to Country. The form can include language, song or dance and varies with the occasion.
SWALSC describes the severe effects of colonisation alongside the persistence of Noongar culture and advocacy. Colonial change did not end Noongar identity.
Community educational posters teach Noongar language through subjects including seasons, plants and bush foods, bringing environmental knowledge into learning resources.
